messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar, a 38-year-old single Middle Eastern man, had always prided himself on his steady hands and keen eye, qualities that made him a sought-after hairdresser in his bustling city salon. His life took an abrupt turn eighteen months ago when a sudden, severe respiratory illness left him fighting for his life in intensive care. He vividly recalled the suffocating panic as tubes were inserted, the acrid, metallic tang of the hospital air, and the searing pain in his chest with every medical procedure. The experience left him deeply shaken, and though his body physically recovered, his mind remained trapped in the ICU.

In the months that followed, Omar found his world shrinking. He discovered that certain triggers now held immense power. Waking up from a nightmare, drenched in sweat and gasping, he would be instantly plunged back into the terror of his illness, his entire body on alert, taut and ready to react to danger that wasn't there. This persistent physical reactivity to dream residue left him exhausted and dreading sleep. Similarly, undergoing a medical examination or procedure, even a routine check-up, would instantly trigger a cascade of memories, often not as clear images but as a profound rush of emotion without image – sheer horror and helplessness that left him trembling. Sometimes, the memory would return with an unsettling olfactory recall, a faint whiff of antiseptic or the metallic scent of blood, instantly transporting him back to the hospital ward. Even innocuous visual cues, such as seeing related photos of hospital rooms or medical equipment on television, could instantly activate his threat response, leaving his body feeling constantly tense and his heart pounding.

These intense reactions began to warp Omar's sense of self. He had come to believe that his body was an enemy, constantly betraying him and reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. This pervasive negative appraisal fueled his sense of threat, keeping his body on alert and hyper-vigilant for any internal or external sign of danger. He started to feel a deep sense of shame about his physical reactions, which further intensified his negative emotions. The constant pain recall, where he would feel physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event when memories returned, cemented his conviction that he could no longer trust his own body. He worried that his escalating fear and physical symptoms meant he was going crazy, a terrifying thought that made him even more fearful of situations that might lead to a physical reaction or an intrusive memory.

Working in the salon became increasingly difficult. The close proximity to clients, the scents of various hair products, and the occasional conversations about health or illness became potent triggers. He found himself avoiding certain clients who reminded him of his time in the hospital, and he'd often excuse himself to the backroom, overwhelmed by a sudden wave of emotion without image, or the phantom smell of hospital disinfectant. His fear that his body was unreliable made him scrutinize every ache or cough, turning minor physical sensations into potential triggers for panic. His apprehension about medical procedures meant he delayed necessary dental work, fearing the enclosed space and the clinical smells would provoke a full-blown panic attack. This constant state of threat, driven by his negative appraisals, led to a tightening loop: the more he believed his body was an enemy, the more his body remained on alert, and the more easily it would react to triggers, bringing back vivid, painful memories. The threat response itself, the constant hypervigilance, made his memories feel even more fragmented and emotionally charged, often presenting as pure emotion rather than concrete images.

Omar finally sought help after a particularly severe episode at work. A client mentioned a friend's recent surgery, and the casual comment, combined with the faint smell of a new hair dye, sent him into a spiral. He felt the familiar pain recall in his chest, his body seizing up, convinced he was relapsing. He retreated to the staff room, overwhelmed by fear and shame, certain he was losing his mind. He recognized then that he couldn't continue living under the constant shadow of his past, perpetually afraid that his own body would betray him, and that every reminder was a precursor to disaster. He desperately wanted to trust his body again and find a way out of the relentless cycle of fear and memory that had consumed his life.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explicitly convey that encountering a trigger directly causes Omar to form or reinforce a negative appraisal about himself or his body.

The vignette describes memories cementing negative appraisals or negative appraisals leading to a fear of memories, but not negative appraisals directly influencing or causing the occurrence or content of intrusive memories.
The vignette demonstrates external stimuli acting as triggers for memories, but it does not convey that the trauma memory itself causally influences or generates new triggers.
